n: This revelation, known as the Word of Wisdom, came after Emma Smith and others were troubled by the tobacco use in the School of the Prophets. It was addressed to the high priests in Kirtland and the Saints in Missouri.

f.g: The School of the Prophets met in the Newel K. Whitney store in Kirtland.

n: At first it was given as wise counsel, not as a strict commandment, to show God’s will for his people’s physical well-being. Later Church leaders made it a firm commandment for members.

f.g: Over time, prophets taught it as binding; today living it is required for baptism and temple worship.

n: It is a principle with a promise, simple enough for even the weakest Saint to live.

f.w: adapted to the capacity of the weak

n: God gives this warning because of the evil intentions of “conspiring men” in the last days—people who would profit from harmful substances.

f.g: Many see a fulfillment in industries that market addictive products.

n: Drinking wine or strong drink is not good or fitting before God, except for the sacrament.
Even sacramental wine should be pure, homemade grape wine. The Lord later allowed other liquids for the sacrament; the Church today uses water.
Alcohol is not for drinking but for washing the body—as in cleaning wounds.

f.g: Stomach; i.e., for eating or drinking.

n: Tobacco is not good for the body; it has limited uses, like treating bruises or sick livestock, used with care and skill.

f.g: Smoked, chewed, or snuffed tobacco was common in 1833 America.

n: “Hot drinks” are not for the body. Early Church leaders explained this means tea and coffee, which remains the Church’s teaching.

f.g: Understood by Church leaders, beginning in the 1830s, to mean tea and coffee.

n: On the positive side, God created wholesome plants for our bodies.
Plants and fruits should be enjoyed in their season, with good judgment and gratitude.
Meat is also given by God for us to use with thanks—but sparingly.
The Lord is pleased when meat is used mainly in winter, cold, or famine.
Grain is the “staff of life”—basic food for people and animals alike.

f.g: A staple food, the support of life (like a walking staff).

n: Wild animals are made for human use only in times of famine and extreme hunger.
All grain is good food, as are fruits of the vine and whatever grows in or above the ground.
Different grains suit different uses: wheat for people, corn for oxen, oats for horses, rye for birds and pigs, and barley for animals and “mild drinks.”

f.g: In older English, often grain generally; in 1830s America, usually maize.
Probably non-intoxicating beverages made from barley.

n: Those who live this law while keeping all the commandments are promised health and strength, down to the core of their bodies.

f.w: health in their navel and marrow to their bones
walking in obedience to the commandments
f.g: The promises depend on overall faithfulness, not diet alone.

n: They will also gain wisdom and great, hidden treasures of knowledge—spiritual blessings, not only physical ones.
They will run without growing weary and walk without fainting—words from Isaiah.
The destroying angel will pass over them as it passed over Israel at the first Passover in Egypt.

f.w: the destroying angel shall pass by them
